doctrine: Production Stack: six sequential pre-production layers that form the foundation for direction work. Layers (in order): 1) Moodboard (3-5 pages: title image, tone, hair/makeup/styling, lighting reference, location reference). 2) Model (confirmed subject matching moodboard look, availability, comfort). 3) Location (scouted at intended time of day, known light, shade available, clean background, backup identified). 4) Set (era filter applied, color math locked to 4-5 color palette values, elevation and depth built, anachronisms removed). 5) Lighting (key/fill/rim setup, hard vs soft choice made, modifiers chosen, grids and flags planned). 6) Pose (seven posing points: feet, knee, hip, torso, shoulders, arms/hands, head/eyes; starting pose plus three variations). Seven Working Rules: 1) Specificity beats breadth. 2) Pre-visit everything that can be pre-visited. 3) Light decides everything else. 4) Subject must know what is happening (send moodboard before). 5) Build the library (database of locations, models, moodboards). 6) One thing done well elevates the shoot. 7) Do not improvise the stack (even when compressed). On-set diagnostic sequence: Light (sun/shadow/fill placement) > Location (background assessment) > Layout (pose). Male posing default recovery: turn body toward light, hands in pockets (thumbs in), feet close, front knee bent, forward lean, chin forward/down. Female posing default recovery: weight shift to one leg, resting leg on tiptoe, one hand at waist/collar/hair, chin down, nose toward light. Three primary lighting setups: A) Window + diffusion bedsheet + white wall fill (natural soft light). B) Two strobes into diffusion panel (frontal key) + beauty dish (top structural light). C) Octabox key + reflector fill + strip softbox rim (classic three-light). Hard light (small source, sharp shadows, reveals texture) vs Soft light (large source, gradient shadows, smooths skin). Modifier grammar: octabox/softbox (default key), beauty dish (medium-hard, reveal structure), strip softbox (elongated highlight for rim), diffusion panel (neutralize hardness), grid (narrow beam, reduce spill), reflector (passive fill), negative fill/poly board (deepen shadow). Short lighting (lit side away from camera, narrower face) vs Broad lighting (lit side toward camera, wider face). Pose vocabulary generated via seven independent points adjusted sequentially. Call sheet consolidates six layers: date/call time, location, shoot duration, moodboard, model contact, team list, wardrobe brief, lighting plan summary, shot list, client contact, weather forecast, contingency location, one-sentence brief. Moodboard is communication first, decoration second. Three audiences: client (can this photographer deliver?), team (technical/stylistic parameters), photographer (locks decision/scope). Board structure is critical: Page 1 (title hero image) carries the entire board on its own merit. Consistency in subsequent pages (repetition of lighting direction, tone, styling) reads stronger than variety. Tools: Pinterest (initial gathering), Cosmos (curated source), Milanote (working board the team receives), Frameset (commercial/film work). Void prompt test with Midjourney/AI: locked moodboard with zero text reveals actual stylistic coherence independent of subject. Scouting discipline: photograph every potential location with phone, note time of day/light character, pin on Google Maps with descriptive label, build legwork database over time. Scouting visit must occur at intended shoot time (not noon default). Check: light at that time, shade density, backgrounds (dark holes/busy distractions/clipping), reflectors (natural bounce surfaces), access (legal/permit), exit strategy (backup location). Persona rule: do not just get Instagram/Facebook, get a real website (huge conversion difference for cold model outreach). Compensation: early portfolio + common look = TFP with delivered images and mutual rights; early portfolio + rare look = pay the rate; established portfolio + any look = pay day rate (professional footing); commercial client = client covers model rate. Portfolio pages: About section, Contact, consistent visual work (Linktree or stale grid loses 80+ percent of conversions). Lighting skin tones: darker tones = meter for face, do not underexpose (underexposure causes fade into background), add 2/3-1 stop compensation, protect face above all. Lighter tones = meter highlights, protect forehead/nose/cheeks, pull key down or diffuse further, meter face. Expose for subject's face regardless of background (background can be blown/crushed). Spot metering on face overrides camera's frame averaging. Mood of frame decided by three variables: light (quality/direction/ratio), background (clean or busy, color relationship), pose (serves frame or fights it). Rule of thirds for portraits: subject on left or right third, face on top third (intersection preferred), subject faces into frame, second anchor element on opposite third line. Symmetrical portraits: face dead center but still on top third vertically. Aperture priority, smallest f-number available (f/2.8, f/1.8, f/1.4), longer focal length, focus on near eye (not nose/cheek). Male pose starters: hands in pockets (thumbs in) + feet close + front knee bent + forward lean + chin down; hand in pocket + hand at collar + body 45-degree angled; hands at sides + body 90-degree turned + head back toward camera. Female pose starters: weight shift + tiptoe + hand at waist + chin down; both hands in hair framing face + slightly angled body; hand at collar + hand at hip + 45-degree turned + eyes past camera. Group posing: every person must have at least one visible arm (no disappearing arms into group). Solutions: one hand pocket/other on shoulder or holding hand, hold hands across group, stagger heights (seated/standing/leaning triangle). Pre-shoot checklist: moodboard locked and sent, model confirmed with address/call time/wardrobe, location scouted at intended time with light/shade/background/backup confirmed, set dressed with era filter/color palette locked, lighting plan on paper (modifiers/stands/grids/flags/batteries), pose vocabulary reviewed (starting pose + three variations per look), call sheet sent day before (not day of), camera/lenses/batteries/cards/backups checked, one-sentence brief written. Word-of-mouth truth: subject who leaves happy with treatment and images becomes repeat referrer and reposting asset; unhappy subject runs machine in reverse. Each shoot is input to pipeline; call sheet + moodboard + in-person experience + delivered images = the product.

workflows: Weekly legwork scouting loop: photograph + label + pin on Google Maps + dump to database
Moodboard workflow: gather on Pinterest > curate on Cosmos > layout on Milanote > test void prompt with AI > lock > deliver to three audiences (client/team/self)
Model outreach workflow: hashtag search or tagged models > send short specific DM + moodboard + portfolio link > get reply > verify website credibility > confirm compensation and usage rights

Location visit workflow: photograph, note time, pin with descriptor > request access if private > visit at intended shoot time > run Light/Location/Layout diagnostic > identify shade, backgrounds, reflectors, exit strategy

On-set sequence: arrive before model > test light without subject > address insecurities in intake > warm up subject body > run Light/Location/Layout for each new spot > cycle through seven posing points, one change at a time > confirm hits > keep beat > meter for face

Post-shoot close: deliver images on time without being asked > thank model > send follow-up DM > save location/setup/pose notes to database > identify one thing that worked best + one thing that failed > loop closes, next shoot begins
prompts: Is there anything you are self-conscious about that you want me to mind while we shoot? (addressed before first pose, matter-of-fact tone, surfaces insecurity, gives permission to address directly)
Can this photographer actually deliver the thing that is in my head? (question moodboard answers for client)
What is the working rhythm that reads as competence? (body-part names instead of left/right, point when possible, confirm hits with 'yes hold that', keep camera off face during direction)
tools: Cosmos (curated home feed, smaller deliberate source pool)
Milanote (layout control, working board the team receives)
Google Maps (pin scouting locations with time/light descriptors)
Model Mayhem, Purple Port (dedicated model casting platforms)
Midjourney (concept visualization with void prompt testing at stylize 100-1000)
Phone camera (location legwork photography and documentation)
operating_rules: The six layers are sequential. Each one narrows the set of decisions the next one has to make.
Light decides everything else. When a layer decision conflicts with the light, the light wins. Every time.
Direction cannot fix what pre-production did not build.
Pre-visit everything that can be pre-visited. Every minute of pre-visit saves ten minutes on the day.
Narrow is the default, not the exception. A moodboard with five images showing the same hard light is more useful than thirty images that disagree.
Do not let later layers bleed into earlier ones.
Run the stack every time, even when the schedule is compressed. A compressed stack is still a stack. A skipped stack is a gamble.
One intentional element set deliberately apart from the baseline is enough to elevate the whole shoot.
The rule is: adjust one point, leave the other six (among the seven posing points). The pose changes with each single adjustment.
The natural pose is the one that photographs worst. The posed stance photographs well.
Meter for the face. Protect the face. Everything else comes second.
Bodies that are standing with nothing to do are hardest to pose. Subjects with a prop (chair/couch/wall/ledge) are easiest.
Subjects who skip the seven-second warm-up pose stiff for the first ten frames and then relax. Subjects who warm up pose relaxed from frame one.
Use body-part names, not left and right. Point when you can. Confirm the hits. Keep the beat. Do not hide behind the camera.
Build the library. The second shoot in any direction should cost a fraction of the first. That only happens if you are saving the work.
Every shoot is an input to the next shoot. The call sheet, the moodboard, the in-person experience, the delivered images. All of it is the product.
A subject who leaves a shoot happy is the single most valuable asset in your pipeline. They will refer, repost, and come back.
If the sentence is hard to write (one-sentence brief), the shoot is not clearly scoped and the issue is upstream of the call sheet.

Male and female posing default recovery sequences (step-by-step physical adjustments)

Lighting setup diagram templates (window-plus-bedsheet, two-strobe-flat-key, classic-key-fill-rim, hard-light-fashion)

Modifier grammar reference card (octabox/beauty-dish/strip-softbox/diffusion/grid/reflector/negative-fill use cases)
Short vs broad lighting decision tree (rounder faces + dramatic need = short, thinner faces + approachability need = broad)
weird_gold: Void prompt test with Midjourney at empty quotation marks reveals actual moodboard coherence independent of subject (cheap diagnostic for fragmented boards before client delivery)
Bedsheet diffusion of midday sun converts hard outdoor light into commercial-grade soft-light setup with zero strobes (cost: the sheet and white wall bounce)
Thumbs inside pockets, fingers outside is the default male pose; thumbs outside with fingers in is the amateur tell
Dappled light (half-shade half-sun across face) guarantees bad frames; full shade or full sun with diffuser only, never half
The rotation trick: forty-five degree rotation = new pose, ninety degree rotation = another new pose, back-to-camera with torso twisted = third new pose (one pose times four rotations is four images)
Metering dark skin tones: underexposure causes fade into background (opposite of lighter tones); add 2/3-1 stop compensation and meter for face without apology
The male default pose (square to camera, hands at crotch) is the worst baseline available; single highest-yield adjustment is bending the front knee slightly
Short vs broad decision controls which side of face is lit relative to camera, not which side the light is placed; change via subject rotation toward or away from key, not by moving the light
